title: How rogue officers turned a nationwide camera network into a tool for stalking

reading.body:
This incident shows an authorized user turning a law enforcement surveillance system to a personal purpose. The failure is not in the license plate reader's accuracy but in oversight of individual queries. The system was used outside the conditions it was built for, which were legitimate police investigations.

Catching this would have required logging every query and reviewing it against the officer's personal relationships, or requiring a second person to approve searches. The reports do not establish that this misuse was widespread or that the department knew of it before the arrest.

reports.title: Kechi police lieutenant arrested for using police technology to stalk wife
Former Kechi police lieutenant convicted on stalking charges
A former police officer has been sentenced in Sedgwick County District Court
‘You were spotted’: KS officer who used police cameras to stalk estranged wife sentenced
Wichita moves to tighten access, increase oversight on secretive police surveillance program
How rogue officers turned a nationwide camera network into a tool for stalking

summary:
Victor Heiar, a lieutenant with the Kechi Police Department, was arrested by Wichita Police after using his access to the police department's license plate reader technology to track his estranged wife's location without permission. Heiar has been charged with one count of stalking and one count of unlawful acts concerning computers, and has been removed from the department and booked into Sedgwick County Jail. A defense attorney noted that officers should never use confidential information and tools for personal purposes, and that repeated monitoring can constitute criminal stalking.

The incident raises concerns about law enforcement properly using surveillance resources, especially given that Wichita and Sedgwick County law enforcement just received 1.6 million dollars in federal funding this week for license plate readers and upgraded camera technology. However, a private investigator stated that while the situation needs to be addressed, such misuse is isolated and does not represent a common problem in police departments, so public safety concerns are minimal.
